query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small titanium addition (~0.5 at.%) into the CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy matrix will trigger in situ formation of a continuous, protective, and lubricious oxide tribofilm during sliding at elevated temperatures, thereby preserving its low friction coefficient and reducing wear rate across the full temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy that, in its baseline state, exhibits low friction and wear at room temperature but suffers from higher friction and accelerated wear at elevated temperatures due to uncontrolled oxide formation and tribochemical reactions.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by adding a minor (~0.5 at.%) Ti element to form a CoCrFeNiTi0.5 alloy.
generation.conditions: Dry sliding wear tests conducted in air under a normal load of approximately 1 N and a sliding speed of about 0.1 m/s over a temperature range from ~25 °C (room temperature) up to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a thin, uniform, and adherent oxide layer that incorporates Ti-rich oxide (e.g., TiO2 or mixed spinel phases) which acts as a self-lubricating tribofilm.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures, the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy performs well; however, upon heating, the minor Ti addition preferentially oxidizes to form a continuous, lubricious oxide film that minimizes direct metal-metal contact during sliding. This film reduces shear forces and stabilizes the friction coefficient while also lowering the wear rate by acting as a barrier against severe abrasion and adhesive wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy, the Ti-doped variant is expected to retain a low coefficient of friction and exhibit significantly reduced wear rates at elevated temperatures (e.g., near 800 °C), while maintaining comparable low friction behavior at room temperature.
generation.baseline: The original CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy, which shows low friction at room temperature but experiences a marked increase in friction coefficient and wear rate above mid-range temperatures (~300–400 °C) due to uncontrolled oxide formation and tribochemical degradation.
generation.boundary: Tests are limited to dry sliding conditions in ambient air with a normal load near 1 N and a sliding speed of about 0.1 m/s, over the temperature interval from approximately 25 °C to 800 °C.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal titanium content and the exact nature (phase composition, thickness, and stability) of the resulting oxide film are not fully defined; additional investigation is required to confirm long-term durability and reliability under cyclic thermal and mechanical loading.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of samples: one of the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy and another of the Ti-doped CoCrFeNiTi0.5 alloy. Conduct standardized dry sliding wear tests under identical conditions (1 N load, 0.1 m/s sliding speed) at several target temperatures (room temperature, ~400 °C, and 800 °C). Use surface analytical techniques to characterize the formation and stability of the oxide tribofilm after sliding.
measurements: Real-time coefficient of friction (COF) as a function of sliding distance
Quantitative wear track depth/volume via profilometry or microscopy
Surface compositional and phase analyses using SEM/EDS and XPS to assess the oxide film characteristics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-doped alloy does not demonstrate a statistically significant lower friction coefficient and reduced wear rate at elevated temperatures (≥400 °C) compared to the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy, or if the expected stable and continuous oxide tribofilm is not detected on the worn surface, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Question: How can a nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film with superior mechanical and tribological properties be synthesized using a cost-effective single target, and what are the effects of annealing on its adhesion and wear performance?. System: Equimolar CuMoTaWV refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates. Processing: DC-magnetron sputtering using a single target prepared by partial spark plasma sintering (SPS) of equimolar elemental powders (Cu, Mo, Ta, W, V) at 1000 °C under 40 MPa pressure; film deposition at 500 °C substrate temperature for 120 min in Ar atmosphere (1.16 × 10⁻³ mPa, 150 W power); post-deposition annealing at 300 °C for adhesion improvement. Test conditions: Nanoindentation at 3 mN load; nanopillar compression (440 nm diameter, 3 mN max force); tribological wear tests at room temperature (RT) and 300 °C with 1 N load and 0.1 m/s sliding speed against E52100 alloy steel counterballs. Question: How does the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy change under reciprocating wear conditions at elevated temperatures, and what are the underlying mechanisms?. System: AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Inert gas atomisation using argon followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1050 °C for 10 min under 50 MPa compaction pressure, with passive cooling at 150 K/min until 300 °C.
